passage:
Dear Charu Ma'am,
You once told me to check my own patterns, so here is a confession. Last month I looked at the task tracker for my team of four. Every tricky client problem had gone to Ankit. Every routine data-cleaning job had gone to Farzana. I never decided that on purpose. It just felt natural, because Ankit "seemed quick" in his first week.
So I changed it. This month all four get one hard problem each, the same fifteen-minute feedback chat every Friday, and the same patience when they ask questions. I'm judging by what they deliver, not by my first impression.
Two weeks in, Farzana's fix for a billing issue was the best in the team. I nearly never found out.
Gratefully,
Rekha

qa.q: What kind of jobs had gone to Farzana?
qa.a: Every routine data-cleaning job.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel on finding that Farzana's fix was the best, and why?
qa.a: Rekha seems relieved and a little shaken ("I nearly never found out"), realising the old pattern would have hidden what Farzana could do.

qa.q: Which changes did Rekha make, and why are they fair?
qa.a: All four now get one hard problem, the same Friday feedback chat and the same patience, and are judged by what they deliver, so no first impression decides anyone's chances.

qa.q: How might Farzana have experienced the months before the change?
qa.a: Farzana kept getting routine jobs without knowing why, and may have felt stuck or overlooked, with no chance to show what Farzana could do.

grounding: A young manager notices hard tasks went to one person and routine ones to another, then gives everyone the same challenge, feedback and patience.

passage: Honestly? What surprised me most in my first year as kitchen manager was me. I'm Deepika, twenty-five, and I run the kitchen at a hotel in Kochi. For months I gave the new dishes to Suresh and the chopping to Farida. When a sauce went wrong, I'd explain it patiently to Suresh and just fix it myself for Farida. One night I watched her standing by the prep counter while Suresh plated my new fish curry, and I thought: when did I decide she couldn't? I had no evidence. So I made a rule. Everyone rotates through the new dishes, everyone gets the same tasting feedback, and I write down what actually happens. Farida's first attempt was average. Her third was the best version we've served.

qa.q: Where does Deepika run the kitchen?
qa.a: At a hotel in Kochi.

qa.q: What was Deepika thinking while watching Farida at the prep counter?
qa.a: Deepika wondered when the decision that Farida couldn't handle new dishes had been made, and realised there was no evidence for it. 🤔

qa.q: Which rule did Deepika make, and why does writing things down matter?
qa.a: Everyone rotates through new dishes with the same tasting feedback, and Deepika records results; writing down what happens means judging by evidence, not impressions.

qa.q: How might the kitchen feel different to Farida after the rotation?
qa.a: Farida finally gets new dishes and real feedback instead of only chopping, so the kitchen can become a place to grow, and her third attempt shows it.

grounding: A young kitchen manager notices a habit of giving new dishes to one cook and chopping to another, then gives everyone the same chances and judges by results.

passage: I'm Jasleen, and I've worked under Rajni at the call centre for a year. In her team meeting last Monday, she did something I've never seen a manager do. She put up the list of who had handled the escalation calls: nine to Varun, none to Gulnaz. Then she said, "I didn't plan that. I think I just expected more from Varun. That isn't fair." From that day, escalations rotate, and each of us gets the same ten minutes of feedback after a hard call. When Gulnaz fumbled her first escalation, Rajni didn't take it back; she listened to the recording with her and let her try again. I don't know what Gulnaz felt, but she asks questions in meetings now, which she never did before.

qa.q: How many escalation calls had gone to Gulnaz?
qa.a: None.

qa.q: Why do you think Rajni showed the list to the whole team?
qa.a: She seemed uncomfortable with an unfair pattern she hadn't planned, and wanted to fix it openly so everyone knew things would change.

qa.q: What choice did Rajni make when Gulnaz fumbled her first escalation, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She didn't take the calls back; she went through the recording with Gulnaz and let her try again, giving her the same patience others had got.

qa.q: How might Varun feel about the change?
qa.a: Varun loses some hard calls and the quiet special status, which might sting a little, though the same fair feedback now applies to Varun as well.

grounding: A colleague watches a young manager admit she gave hard calls to one person and none to another, then rotate them with equal feedback and patience.

passage:
Monday: Jeevan, twenty-six and newly made site supervisor, sat with the weekly plan for the housing project in Nashik. Slab inspection: Arvind. Structural checks: Arvind. Paperwork and material register: Rashmi. He frowned. Rashmi had the same degree and the same six months on site. Why had he done that? He couldn't find a reason, only a feeling.
Three weeks later: he rotated the plan. Rashmi got the third-floor slab inspection. She missed a crack near a column, and Jeevan walked her to it and explained, slowly, the way he always did with Arvind. She wrote it down and thanked him.
Two months later: at the review, Jeevan pulled out the inspection logs instead of trusting his impressions. Rashmi's were the most detailed on the site. Arvind's were good but rushed. Jeevan put both names on the next tower and wrote in his notebook: check the list, not the feeling.

qa.q: What did Rashmi miss during her first slab inspection?
qa.a: She missed a crack near a column.

qa.q: How did Jeevan feel when he looked at the weekly plan on Monday?
qa.a: He felt uneasy, frowning when he saw he had given Arvind all the tough work for no reason but a feeling, though Rashmi had the same degree and experience.

qa.q: Which of Jeevan's choices made the plan fairer, and why?
qa.a: He rotated the tough tasks, gave Rashmi the same patient explanation he gave Arvind, and judged them later by their logs, not his impressions.

qa.q: How might Rashmi have seen the change in her work?
qa.a: Rashmi probably felt trusted and taken seriously for the first time, getting real inspections and patient feedback instead of only paperwork.

grounding: A young site supervisor notices he hands tough work to one engineer and routine work to another, then gives both the same challenge and patience and judges by the logs.

passage: Parul, you've just been made team lead and you're asking me how to be fair. Let old Vasudha tell you her mistake. At twenty-five I was made head of the primary section at a school in Indore, the youngest in the staffroom. That first year, I gave the science exhibition, the inspection lessons and the parents' meetings to Mrs Joshi, because she spoke well. Mrs Rao got the attendance and the timetable. In March I made the list for the annual report and saw it written down. I felt quite ashamed. I had never once watched Mrs Rao teach. So the next year, I made a rotation. Everyone got a big project, everyone got my notes, everyone got the same patience when things went wrong. And I looked at results, children's work, not at who sounded confident. Mrs Rao's class did the best model at the exhibition. Write your list down, Parul. The list doesn't lie.

qa.q: What did Mrs Rao's class do at the next exhibition?
qa.a: Mrs Rao's class did the best model at the exhibition.

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel on seeing the list written down?
qa.a: Vasudha felt quite ashamed, seeing that one teacher had got everything big and the other only routine work, without ever being watched teaching.

qa.q: What changes did Vasudha make, and how can Parul use them?
qa.a: Vasudha rotated the big projects, gave everyone the same notes and patience, and judged by children's work; Parul can write down the team's task list and do the same.

qa.q: How might Mrs Rao have felt in that first year?
qa.a: Mrs Rao may have felt overlooked and underused, handling attendance and timetables while someone else got all the chances to shine.

grounding: A retired head tells a new lead how they once noticed giving the big tasks to one teacher and routine work to another, then gave all the same challenge and judged by results.

passage:
Half of Lalit's team was down with flu, and the product launch was in four days. As he assigned tasks on the whiteboard, he stopped with the marker in the air.
Tanuja: database migration, client demo, bug triage. Harish: meeting notes, test data, meeting notes again.
He looked back through the last three months. Every hard task had gone to Tanuja. Harish had never been given one. Lalit realised he had decided early that Harish was "steady but not strong", and had never checked.
There was no time for a big fix, but he could do something. He moved the client demo to Harish and blocked thirty minutes that evening to rehearse it with him. "Ask me anything," he said.
Harish's demo on Friday was nervous but solid. Lalit wrote down what went well and what didn't, the same way he did for Tanuja.

qa.q: How many days were there until the product launch?
qa.a: The product launch was in four days.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling when he stopped with the marker in the air?
qa.a: Lalit felt uncomfortable and a little guilty, realising he had been handing all the hard tasks to Tanuja without ever testing Harish.

qa.q: Which of Lalit's steps show him judging by evidence rather than expectation?
qa.a: He gave Harish a real challenge, gave rehearsal time and support, and then wrote feedback on the demo the same way he did for Tanuja.

qa.q: How might Harish see being given the client demo?
qa.a: Harish may feel surprised and nervous, but also trusted for the first time, which could change how he sees his own ability.

grounding: A manager under time pressure notices he gives hard tasks to one person and routine ones to another, and deliberately gives both the same challenge and feedback.

passage:
On a Monday in the hospital's billing office in Kolkata, Jeevan, the new supervisor, was reviewing the month's assignments on his screen. Complex insurance cases: all to Sayantan. Simple receipts: all to Nirmala.
He frowned. Nirmala had been there longer. Why had he never given her a complex case? He thought back. On her first day she had asked a lot of questions, and he'd filed her as "needs hand-holding."
He called her over. "From this week, you and Sayantan split the complex cases evenly. I'll review both of your files the same way, same time, every Friday."
Nirmala hesitated. "Are you sure?"
"I'm sure I don't know yet. That's the point."
By the third Friday, Nirmala's files had fewer errors than Sayantan's. Jeevan noted it, surprised, and kept the split.

qa.q: Who had been given all the complex insurance cases?
qa.a: All the complex insurance cases went to Sayantan.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling when he frowned at the screen?
qa.a: Jeevan felt uneasy and doubtful about his own judgement, realising he had filed Nirmala as "needs hand-holding" after one day.

qa.q: Why did splitting the cases evenly help Jeevan judge fairly?
qa.a: Giving both the same challenges and the same Friday review let real evidence, not his first impression, show who did well.

qa.q: How might Nirmala feel after being given complex cases?
qa.a: Nirmala may feel nervous at first but also respected, and proud when her files had fewer errors.

grounding: A supervisor notices he gives complex work to one clerk and routine work to another, then splits them evenly and judges by evidence.

passage:
"Irfan, got a minute?" Jaya pulled out the chair beside his desk.
"Sure. Did I mess up the report?"
"No. That's the thing. I was going through the quarter. I gave Sneh the partner pitch, the budget model and the hiring panel. You got the report formatting and the meeting bookings."
"It's fine. Sneh's good at that stuff."
"Maybe. But I never gave you the chance to be. I decided that in your first week, and I think that was unfair."
Irfan was quiet. "So what now?"
"Next pitch is yours. Sneh takes the bookings for once. You'll get the same review from me that she gets, line by line, and the same time to fix it."
"And if I'm bad at it?"
"Then we'll know from the work, not from my guess."

qa.q: What three tasks had Jaya given Sneh this quarter?
qa.a: Jaya gave Sneh the partner pitch, the budget model and the hiring panel.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling when he asked "Did I mess up the report?"
qa.a: Irfan felt anxious and a bit unsure, expecting criticism rather than a new chance.

qa.q: What did Jaya do to judge Irfan by evidence rather than guesswork?
qa.a: Jaya gave him the next pitch, promised the same line-by-line review and fixing time Sneh gets, and said the work, not a guess, would decide.

qa.q: How might Sneh feel about taking the bookings for once?
qa.a: Sneh might feel surprised or a bit put out at first, but it also takes pressure off always being the one given big tasks.

grounding: A manager realises having given all the tough work to one person and routine work to another, and deliberately gives both the same challenge and feedback.

passage:
I'm Farida, twenty-six and managing a team for the first time, and in March I made a spreadsheet of who got which assignment. It was uncomfortable. Every hard client, every new project, had gone to Ankur, who talks fast in meetings. Every routine report had gone to Nilesh, who is quiet. I had never decided that on purpose. I had just "known" Ankur was the strong one.
So I changed the system. Hard projects now rotate. Everyone gets the same written feedback within two days, and I judge by the finished work, not by how confident someone sounds.
Nilesh's first client proposal was slow and careful, and it was the best one we sent that quarter. When Ankur had a rough month, I gave him the same patience.

qa.q: What did Farida make a spreadsheet of?
qa.a: Who got which assignment.

qa.q: How did Farida feel looking at the spreadsheet?
qa.a: Farida felt uncomfortable and a bit ashamed, seeing a pattern of expectations that had never been chosen on purpose.

qa.q: Which changes made Farida's system fairer?
qa.a: Rotating hard projects, giving everyone the same written feedback, and judging finished work rather than confidence.

qa.q: How might Nilesh have experienced the change?
qa.a: After months of routine reports, a client proposal may have felt like being trusted at last, and he rose to it.

grounding: Shows a new manager noticing she gave tough work to one person and routine work to another, then giving everyone the same challenge and feedback and judging by results.

passage:
Kitchen note, end of month. Dolma, head chef.
I asked Darshan, our new sous chef, to plan the Diwali rotas. In his first draft, every tricky station, the tandoor and the sauces, went to Rakesh. Chitra and Beena had only prep. I didn't say anything; I waited.
Two days later he came back. "I looked again. I've been giving Rakesh everything because he's loud and sure of himself. That's not evidence." He rewrote it: everyone rotates through the hard stations, and everyone gets the same five-minute feedback after service.
After three weeks, Beena runs the sauce station better than anyone. I will recommend Darshan for the permanent post.

qa.q: Which stations did Rakesh get in the first draft?
qa.a: The tandoor and the sauces, every tricky station.

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling when he came back two days later?
qa.a: He seemed uneasy but honest, bothered to see that confidence, not evidence, had shaped his choices.

qa.q: What did Darshan's rewrite do well?
qa.a: It gave everyone turns at the hard stations and equal feedback, so real skill could show, as Beena's did.

qa.q: How might Beena feel after three weeks at the sauce station?
qa.a: She likely feels proud and trusted, finally given a real chance to show her skill.

grounding: A head chef's note shows a young manager catching himself handing hard work to one confident person and giving everyone the same challenge and feedback instead.

passage:
Thursday night.
Performance chats today. Halfway through Jatin's, I realised I had decided what to say before he walked in: "solid, reliable, not a leader". Why? Because in month one he missed a deadline. That's it. Since then I've given him the routine work and saved the big launch for Meghna.
So I stopped and asked him what he wanted to work on. He said, "I'd like to try leading the vendor calls." I nearly said "maybe later".
New rule for me: before I assign anything, I write down why, and check it's based on the last three months, not the first week. And Jatin leads the vendor call on Monday, with the same prep time and the same feedback Meghna gets.
Shreya

qa.q: What did Jatin want to try?
qa.a: Leading the vendor calls.

qa.q: How did Shreya feel halfway through Jatin's chat?
qa.a: Shreya felt uneasy and a little guilty, noticing the verdict had been decided before Jatin walked in.

qa.q: Why is Shreya's new rule a good check?
qa.a: Writing down the reason and basing it on recent months makes assignments rest on evidence, not an old first impression.

qa.q: How might Jatin feel leading Monday's call?
qa.a: He may feel nervous but valued, finally given the same chance and support as Meghna.

grounding: A young manager's diary shows noticing an unfair expectation of one team member and deliberately giving him the same challenge and feedback, judged by evidence.

passage: After the evening collection at the milk cooperative in Sangola, Ramesh sat with the duty register and frowned. Fat testing, machine repairs, the argument with the transporter: all Akash. The ledgers and the sweeping of the cooling room: always Nilesh. Only last week Ramesh had called Nilesh 'slow' to his wife. But when had the boy ever been given a problem to be slow at? Next morning he tore out a fresh page. 'From today we rotate,' he told both young men. 'Tuesday Nilesh tests the fat and Akash does the ledgers. I'll stand beside whoever is testing, same as I did for Akash last year.' On Tuesday Nilesh fumbled the first sample and went red. Ramesh only said, 'Again, slower.' By Friday Nilesh's readings matched the lab's. Ramesh wrote the readings down, not his opinion.

qa.q: In which town is the milk cooperative?
qa.a: Sangola.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh frown over the duty register?
qa.a: Ramesh felt uneasy and a little guilty, seeing that every hard job went to Akash and that he had called Nilesh 'slow' without ever giving him a real problem.

qa.q: What did Ramesh do that a supervisor elsewhere could copy?
qa.a: Rotate the hard and routine jobs, stand beside whoever is learning with the same patience, and record actual results rather than an opinion.

qa.q: How might Nilesh have felt when he fumbled the first sample and heard only 'Again, slower'?
qa.a: Nilesh was embarrassed at first, but the calm reply told him he was trusted to learn, which helped his readings match the lab's by Friday.

grounding: A supervisor notices he gives tough tasks to one worker and routine ones to another, then shares challenge and patience equally and judges by results.

passage: Kofi noticed it on a wet Tuesday in Toronto, halfway through writing the week's job board at the bike shop. Wheel builds: Hannah. Hydraulic brakes: Hannah. The e-bike motor nobody understood: Hannah again. Beside Javier's name were flat tyres and chain cleans, the same as last month. Kofi put the marker down. Javier had never ruined a wheel build. He had never been handed one. Kofi wiped half the board and split the hard jobs down the middle. At lunch he told Javier, 'You're on the touring wheel. It'll take you longer than Hannah, and that's fine. Bring it to me before it goes out.' Javier's first wheel wobbled. Kofi showed him the spoke tension twice, slowly, the way he had once shown Hannah. The second wheel ran true, and Kofi wrote that on the board.

qa.q: Which jobs were beside Javier's name on the board?
qa.a: Flat tyres and chain cleans, the same as last month.

qa.q: What does Kofi putting the marker down suggest about his feelings?
qa.a: It suggests he felt uncomfortable and a little ashamed, realising Javier had never been given a hard job to succeed or fail at.

qa.q: How could Kofi keep things fair in the coming months?
qa.a: He could keep splitting the hard jobs evenly, give both mechanics the same patient explanations, and judge them by how their finished work rides.

qa.q: What is it like for Javier when his first wheel wobbles?
qa.a: Javier may feel embarrassed and unsure, but because Kofi explains the spoke tension patiently instead of taking the job away, he gets a real chance to improve.

grounding: Shows a manager spotting that challenging work always goes to one person, then sharing challenge and patience evenly and judging by the finished work.
